images.title: Can this job be packaged?
images.alt: Decision chart: if you can list the job's steps without saying it depends, check your hours; if not, keep it as custom work.
images.caption: Your first offer is usually narrower than you expect, like a five-email welcome sequence instead of marketing help.

data.question: Can you write the steps as a numbered list without "it depends"?

branches.result: Compare hours: if the slowest took three times the fastest, one price will hurt
Too variable to package. Keep it as custom work with a quote

images.after: How to say no to out-of-scope requests
images.title: Three answers to out-of-scope requests
images.alt: Four cards: offer an add-on, quote a separate project, refer it on, and keep a list of priced add-ons for common requests.
images.caption: Deciding your answers in advance means you aren't inventing them under pressure.

items.title: It's an add-on
items.text: Name a price for the extra and ask if they want it added

items.title: It's a separate project
items.text: Offer a custom quote once the current package is finished

items.title: It's not something you do
items.text: Say so, and point them to the kind of person who does

items.title: Keep a priced add-on list
items.text: Covers the requests you hear most and makes yes or no easy

images.title: Delivering the same way every time
images.alt: Flow of a productized service delivery: payment and agreement, intake form, confirmed date, work from your list, then check, deliver and close.
images.caption: Writing down the work step in detail is what later lets you speed up or hand routine parts to an assistant.

items.label: Pay and accept
items.text: Client pays and accepts the agreement

items.label: Intake form
items.text: Client sends access, files and goals

items.label: Confirm and date
items.text: You confirm you have it all and give the delivery date

items.label: Check, deliver, close
items.text: Check against "what you get", handle the revision, ask for feedback
